items.title: Myth-Busting Pulse Dose Steroid for Non-CNS Indications
items.summary: Farkas argues there is no justification for ≥500mg methylprednisolone outside CNS disease, which is a call you may be asked to sign off on this week.
items.note: Pulse dosing is one of those things that gets escalated to almost reflexively when a patient on 1–2 mg/kg prednisone fails to improve, and Farkas's point is that the escalation is pharmacologically illogical rather than merely aggressive. He puts numbers on the downside — cardiotoxicity and invasive fungal infection — and suggests adding or switching immunomodulator instead. Useful for the conversations that happen at the ICU door rather than in the ED itself.

items.title: A New Definition of Myocardial Infarction: What's Changed
items.summary: The Fifth Universal Definition rewrites the MI classification you document under, read here by an Australian EM site rather than a cardiology one.
items.note: The numbered Type 1–5 system is gone, replaced by primary, secondary and procedure-related, and MINOCA is now myocardial *injury* rather than infarction. The line this piece hammers is the one that bites hardest in an Australian ED: an elevated troponin is injury, not infarction, and sepsis, PE, heart failure, anaemia and tachyarrhythmia all raise it. Complements the St Emlyn's read on the same guideline from a few weeks back, from a source that shares your case mix.

items.title: Ultrasound Case 109
items.summary: A six-year-old with a week of intermittent lower abdominal pain, already labelled mesenteric adenitis — scan it yourself before reading on.
items.note: The POCUS Top 100 series is the closest free thing to CCPU practice cases, and this one is a paediatric abdomen with a pre-existing diagnostic label attached, which is exactly the setup where a bedside scan either confirms or overturns someone else's thinking. Case 108 was in the feed a few days ago; this is the next in sequence.

items.title: CXR Case 138
items.summary: A routine post-procedure ICU chest film with a nasogastric tube where it should not be — the cheapest possible rehearsal for a real one.
items.note: NG malposition is the kind of finding that is obvious once seen and catastrophic when missed, and the only reliable way to make it obvious is to have looked at a stack of them. LITFL's CXR Top 100 runs the same self-assessment format as the ECG series you already work through, so the drill is familiar.

items.title: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and a New Price War
items.summary: Two frontier releases ninety minutes apart and a coordinated price cut — the clearest single read on what changed this week in AI.
items.note: Willison has the numbers rather than the vibes: Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 per million with cached reads down 60% to $0.20, and GPT-6 Luna launching at $0.10/$0.50. He also notes which models he has actually switched his own defaults to, which is a more honest signal than any benchmark table. Worth reading because the pricing floor is what decides whether the AI tooling around your work is a subscription or an afterthought.

items.title: What Australian GPs Should Consider Before Adopting AI Scribes
items.summary: The RACGP has put a position statement around AI scribes, including the requirement that a human read every note before it enters the record.
items.note: Metro South's rollout across five Queensland hospitals was in the feed recently as a deployment story; this is the governance side of the same wave, and Victorian health services will land on the same questions shortly. The human-review requirement is the part that matters for anyone who will eventually be signing an AI-drafted ED note. Consent, storage and what happens to the audio are the other three.

items.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez Trace Their Roots on 'Los Ojos Del Cóndor'
items.summary: The third Auerbach-produced record from a duo already on your shelf, out today, and this is the review that actually describes the playing.
items.note: Hermanos Gutiérrez are in the library, so this is a new pressing for a shelf that already has them rather than a recommendation from cold. The ten tracks swap the American-West reverb of the earlier records for Andean instrumentation — charango, moaning organ, lap steel — which is a real shift rather than a repeat, and it sits close to the Glass Beams and Khruangbin end of the collection. No Depression is new to the feed and writes about instrumental records better than most.

items.title: Just a Simple Picture: A One Shot Story
items.summary: One frame, one essay — the format that gets closer to why a photograph works than any technique piece manages.
items.note: 35mmc's One Shot Story series is built on the discipline of defending a single negative, which is a better exercise than another emulsion review. 'A Study in Deep Shade' from earlier this month came through the same series, so the format has landed before.

items.title: First Look: Tiny Bar in Brunswick East Has Expert Snacks
items.summary: A French Saloon chef has gone small and local — wine-bar cooking at proper standard, a short ride up Lygon Street.
items.note: Brunswick East has had a run of these lately — Tenko on Lygon, Better Now, Scroll Lab in Brunswick West — but this one brings a CBD fine-dining kitchen down to snack scale, which is the version worth walking to. Broadsheet's First Look pieces get their own URL rather than being folded into a monthly roundup, so the detail on what is actually on the plate survives.

items.title: Abandoned Republic: A Journey Through Vintage BR Catalogs
items.summary: Fifteen years of scanned Banana Republic Travel & Safari catalogues — the primary source behind a reference point you already use.
items.note: Vintage Banana Republic sits on the short list of touchstones for this kind of wardrobe, and almost everything written about it is secondhand nostalgia. Robyn Adams has instead archived the actual catalogues from the Ziegler era, essays, illustrations and travel dispatches included, so you can see how the garments were drawn and sold rather than how they are resold now. Useful the next time something bush-jacket-shaped turns up in a Melbourne op shop and you need to date it.

items.title: Kuldra's Saga — The Roadmap Update
items.summary: Jagex's first-party post-1.0 plan: Prayer as the thirteenth skill in December, and a 1.0.1 in October.
items.note: You followed the 1.0 launch and the 1.0.0.5 hotfix through the feed, so this is the answer to what comes after the corrupted-saves firefighting. Luminance lands in December with Prayer — bury bones, build an altar, toggle passives — plus a new material tier and a region beyond the Scorned Wilderness, with Magic Tree Seeds arriving in October's 1.0.1. First-party, so the dates are Jagex's own rather than a wiki's reading of them.

items.title: GTA 6's Wanted System Goes Up to Six Stars
items.summary: Rockstar has rebuilt pursuit around witnesses and identification rather than omniscient cops — the first mechanical detail worth caring about.
items.note: Six stars is the first time since Chinatown Wars, but the real change is the Red Dead 2 import: no crime is reported unless someone sees it or an alarm goes off, and police then track your face, clothes, car and whether you had company. That makes masks and outfit changes actual mechanics rather than cosmetics. Fifty-odd days out from 19 November, this is the kind of system detail that tells you how the game will play rather than how it looks.
